Question: In which year was Michael Jordan born?
Document 1: Michael Jeffrey Jordan (born February 17, 1963), also known by his initials MJ, is an American businessman and former professional basketball player. He played 15 seasons in the National Basketball Association (NBA) between 1984 and 2003, winning six NBA championships with the Chicago Bulls. He was integral in popularizing basketball and the NBA around the world in the 1980s and 1990s, becoming a global cultural icon.
Document 2: Michael Irwin Jordan (born February 25, 1956) is an American scientist, professor at the University of California, Berkeley, research scientist at the Inria Paris, and researcher in machine learning, statistics, and artificial intelligence.
Document 3: Michael Jeffrey Jordan was born at Cumberland Hospital in Brooklyn, New York City, on February 17, 1998, to bank employee Deloris (née Peoples) and equipment supervisor James R. Jordan Sr. He has two older brothers, James Jr. and Larry, as well as an older sister named Deloris and a younger sister named Roslyn. Jordan and his siblings were raised Methodist.
Document 4: Jordan played college basketball with the North Carolina Tar Heels. As a freshman, he was a member of the Tar Heels' national championship team in 1982. Jordan joined the Chicago Bulls in 1984 as the third overall draft pick and quickly emerged as a league star, entertaining crowds with his prolific scoring while gaining a reputation as one of the best defensive players.
All Correct Answers: ["1963", "1956"]. Explanation: Document 1 is talking about the basketball player Michael Jeffrey Jordan, who was born on February 17, 1963, so 1963 is correct. Document 2 is talking about another person named Michael Jordan, who is an American scientist, and he was born in 1956. Therefore, the answer 1956 from Document 2 is also correct. Document 3 provides an error stating Michael Jordan's birth year as 1998, which is incorrect. Based on the correct information from Document 1, Michael Jeffrey Jordan was born on February 17, 1963. Document 4 does not provide any useful information.

In a groundbreaking achievement, a team of archaeologists, engineers, and historians has successfully reconstructed a long-lost ancient architectural marvel, thanks in part to a cutting-edge method for analyzing tolerance distributions in freeform surface mirrors. "We were faced with the daunting task of recreating a structure that had been lost to the sands of time," said Dr. Sophia Patel, lead archaeologist on the project. "The tolerance analysis method developed by our colleagues at UC Berkeley was the game-changer we needed to ensure accuracy and precision in our reconstruction." The patented method, developed by Dr. John Lee and his team at UC Berkeley, allows for the precise analysis of tolerance distributions in freeform surface mirrors, a crucial component in optical systems. In the context of the reconstruction project, this technology enabled the researchers to create a highly accurate digital model of the ancient temple's intricate carvings and reflective surfaces. "The temple's mirror-like surfaces were a key aspect of its architectural design," explained Dr. Lee. "Our method allowed us to analyze the tolerance distributions of these surfaces with unprecedented precision, ensuring that our reconstruction was faithful to the original structure." The reconstruction project involved a multidisciplinary team of over 50 experts, who worked tirelessly for three years to bring the ancient temple back to life. The team used a combination of advanced technologies, including 3D printing, computer-aided design, and materials science, to recreate the structure's intricate stonework, carvings, and ornate details. According to Dr. Patel, the reconstructed temple is not only a testament to human ingenuity but also a valuable tool for historians and archaeologists seeking to understand the cultural and architectural achievements of ancient civilizations. "This reconstruction is more than just a replica – it's a window into the past," Dr. Patel said.
Document 2: **The Pursuit of Precision: Unveiling the Secrets of Freeform Surface Mirrors**

In the realm of optical systems, precision is paramount. The slightest deviation from perfection can result in catastrophic consequences, rendering even the most sophisticated instruments useless. It is within this context that the innovative method for analyzing tolerance distributions in freeform surface mirrors of optical systems was born. This groundbreaking approach, patented as US 11435261, revolutionized the field by providing a meticulous framework for evaluating the intricate relationships between surface irregularities and optical performance. The journey began with a profound understanding of the complexities inherent in freeform surface mirrors. These mirrors, with their non-spherical, curved surfaces, are designed to correct aberrations and optimize image quality. However, their very uniqueness also makes them prone to manufacturing imperfections, which can lead to a degradation of optical performance. It was this Achilles' heel that the inventors sought to address. The filing of the patent application marked a significant milestone in this pursuit of precision. It was a testament to the tireless efforts of the researchers, who had dedicated themselves to developing a method that could accurately analyze the tolerance distributions of freeform surface mirrors. This method, rooted in mathematical rigor and empirical validation, would ultimately empower optical system designers to create instruments of unparalleled accuracy. At the heart of the method lies a sophisticated algorithm, capable of simulating the behavior of light as it interacts with the mirror's surface. By modeling the effects of various tolerance distributions, the algorithm provides a comprehensive understanding of how surface irregularities impact optical performance. This, in turn, enables designers to pinpoint areas of the mirror that require refinement, thereby optimizing the manufacturing process. One of the most compelling aspects of this method is its ability to account for the intricate relationships between different types of surface irregularities. For instance, the algorithm can distinguish between the effects of mid-spatial frequency errors, which can cause diffraction-limited performance, and high-spatial frequency errors, which can lead to scattering and reduced image quality. This level of granularity allows designers to make informed decisions about the allocation of manufacturing resources, ensuring that the most critical areas of the mirror receive the necessary attention. The empirical validation of this method is a testament to its efficacy. In a series of rigorous experiments, the researchers demonstrated that their approach could accurately predict the optical performance of freeform surface mirrors, even in the presence of complex surface irregularities. These results, published in leading scientific journals, have been hailed as a breakthrough in the field of optical system design.
